thread.title: Health Care Is Alive And Well At CES

author: Barron's
title: Health Care Is Alive And Well At CES
text:
LAS VEGAS - Music legend Lionel Richie is an unlikely pitchman for a newfangled medical device at the sprawling Consumer Electronics Show in Las Vegas this week.
Such is the eclectic field of health-care technology, which is morphing in many shapes and forms as commercial ventures explore the possibilities of artificial intelligence, robotics and vast amounts of data.
Getty Images From smartphone apps and small devices to a life-sized robot, CES saw its fair share of technology solutions. Tech's reshaping of large swaths of the multibillion-dollar industry are most likely to manifest in wearables, robots, sensors and AI, concluded a panel on the topic called "The Invisible Doctor." Another wild card: Amazon.com's (ticker: AMZN ) anticipated entry into the pharmacy market.
Growth projections for the health-care/tech market are plentiful, making it hard to put a definitive figure on what most experts agree is an enormous market. In the most recently available information, market researcher Euromonitor International pegged global sales of consumer health products at $217 billion in 2016, up 3% from 2015.
"Everybody is coming after health care because it is sloshing in money, probably trillions of dollars," says Girish Venkatachaliah , a former IBM Watson Health executive who is now vice president of machine learning at AthenaHealth ( ATHN ). " Apple ( AAPL ), [Alphabet's] ( GOOGL ) Google, Amazon and IBM ( IBM ) are circling the industry. It will only amplify in the coming months."
The rub is that modifying - if not revising - health care is hard. Obstacles, in the form of a fragmented health-care industry that is also heavily regulated, are formidable, says Venkatachaliah.
CES is a crude if not glorified lab for what the health-care industry may look like in 10 years as medical professionals attempt to get a handle on a growing mountain of data in the digital age. Perhaps it might even narrow the grand divide between tech-savvy consumers and the analog-driven doctors, dentists and optometrists they go to, says Shoshana Ungerleider , a doctor in San Francisco who advises medical tech startups.
"I'm super bullish on medical technology but most of it exists in doctor's offices, not in the house - that's several years away," counters Adrian Aoun , a former Alphabet executive who co-founded Forward , which has designed state-of-the-art medical facilities in the U.S. that combine several examination rooms equipped with interactive displays and two body scanners that collect data via wearable sensors.
Health-care solutions are alive and well at CES in multiple forms:
Apps. Richie, an Academy Award- and Grammy-winning songwriter, is touting Heal , an on-demand house call app that is teaming with Qualcomm ( QCOM ) on something called Heal Wellbe . The device, which looks like a plug-in light, wirelessly connects to health-care sensors to log vital signs such as pulse, blood pressure and heart rate.
Richie wasn't in Vegas this week, but in a recent phone interview he said he's an investor in Heal because he's a big believer in what technology can do to bring efficiency to an antiquated health-care field. So far, Heal has delivered 40,000 house calls nationwide in less than three years.
"It is a natural extension of our primary (out-call) service," says Heal CEO Nick Desai . It also underscores, he says, how health care is at the "forefront of how technology can change our lives."
Meanwhile, Concierge Key Health is in the early stages of building an Uber-like health service nationwide, with an app that lets consumers schedule appointments, on-demand, with top-tier physicians and general practitioners in orthopedics, cardiology and other specialized fields.
So far, patients in a dozen cities including New York and Los Angeles have the ability to digitally book appointments from a pool of 1,500 specialists for urgent care and hospital concierge clinics.
The Newport Beach, Calif.-based startup joins telehealth firm Curely and others developing apps designed to match patients and physicians at a time when the healthcare industry wrestles with a primary care shortage.
From the hardware side, comes French company Cutti's life-size autonomous robot companion for seniors. Mounted with a touchscreen and equipped with facial- and speech-recognition technology, Cutti is intended to connect seniors with friends, family and healthcare providers. It can also take them via the screen to activities such as yoga classes, museum visits and cooking lessons.
Devices. Bowhead Health has developed an ecosystem in the shape of a squat cylindrical box that houses at-home health tests and a blockchain-based health data-management system.
Mira Fertility demonstrated a personalized ovulation system leveraging AI that helps couples conceive. And Cocoon Cam introduced Clarity by Cocoon Cam, its advanced baby monitor and site, www.cocooncam.com/clarity.
Reliefband , a watch-like contraption, offers a drug-free solution for nausea associated with motion sickness, VR activity, chemotherapy and pregnancy.
Finally, PhoneSoap - a disinfectant that doubles as a wireless charger - was on display at the Health & Wellness Marketplace. "Guaranteed to avoid the CES flu," its marketing materials breathlessly promised.
Only at CES.
